newsitem.title: Switzerland: U.S. sees good chance of success at telecoms talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees good chance of success at telecoms talks.

text.p: A top U.S. negotiator signalled on Friday Washington was ready to sign up by a Saturday deadline to a global pact opening up the worldwide basic telecommunications industry to competition.

"We have a good possibility of success," Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang told reporters after a meeting at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) of delegates from the 61 countries in the talks to assess prospects for a deal.

"We are making progress and can see the way forward," Lang added. Another U.S. official said there would be no extension of talks beyond February 15, declaring: "We are not going to go beyond tomorrow (Saturday)."

And although the U.S. announced at the WTO session it was adding restrictions on transmission of some television and audio services to its offer on the table, other trading powers made clear they were still ready for an accord.

"It looks like there is a deal," Chief Canadian negotiator Michael Binder told reporters, although trade diplomats said the restrictions were primarily aimed at Ottawa whose own offer was strongly criticised by Washington.

European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said ministers from the 15 EU member states, who met after the WTO session to discuss the package of offers from 61 countries, "have decided to go along with the agreement....
"The agreement as a whole is a huge success for the WTO. We feel the benefits to world trade will be enormous," he declared.

WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero also expressed cautious optimism on prospects for the pact, which is expected to slash telephone costs for ordinary people and businesses around the globe and give a major boost to the telecom equipment industry.

"We are not far from a good result, but it is too early to be certain," he said. Ruggiero has set success in the telecoms talks -- left over from the 1986-93 Uruguay Round of world trade negotiations -- as top priority for the fledgling body.

Negotiators set another meeting for 2.30 p.m. in Geneva (1330GMT) on Saturday at which diplomats from all participating countries were likely to say whether they formally accepted the package now on the table and would sign a pact.
Officials in Washington said Acting Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky would call a news conference during the day, apparently to announce the final U.S. decision.

Earlier, Brittan joined officials from other trading powers in urging the United States -- vital for a pact as it is the world's largest single telecom market -- to come on board and not walk away as it did from an earlier bid last April.
"What is on the table amounts to a massive liberalisation of the world telecommunication market that it would be crazy not to grab with both hands," he told a news conference.
"I see no conceivable justification on the basis of what is on the table for failing to clinch the deal," he added.

EU officials said the newly-announced U.S. restrictions -- applying to one-way satellite transmissions of some television services and digital audio services -- appeared to violate Washington's commitments under the Uruguay Round accords.

But they said the EU had been assured, apparently in a telephone call between Brittan and Barshefsky late on Friday, that these measures, which would leave open an option to treat trading partners differently, would not be applied to it.
